items.title: U.S. Navy Veteran Revisits South Korea Through the Revisit Korea Program
items.author: SGT Kourtney Nunnery
items.summary: U.S. Navy veteran, Dr. Daniel Frenning revisits South Korea through the Revisit Korea Program orchestrated by the Republic of Korea government to thank the service members from the U.S. who have served in South Korea.
items.body: COMMANDER FLEET ACTIVITIES, CHINHAE, SOUTH KOREA- U.S. Navy veteran, Dr. Daniel Frenning revisits South Korea through the Revisit Korea Program orchestrated by the Republic of Korea government to thank the service members from the U.S. who have served in South Korea. Dr. Frenning was commissioned as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps in 1972 and was assigned as the chief general medical officer at Commander Fleet Activities Chinhae (CFAC) in South Korea. Because his assignment was accompanied, his wife, Carol, was able to reside with him in Chinhae. The Frennings arrived during a transformative period in South Korean history. The years between1972–1974 were defined by two major developments: the establishment of the authoritarian Yushin system, which centralized political power and suppressed democratic opposition, and the rapid expansion of heavy and chemical industrialization, which established the country's modern economic and corporate infrastructure. Within this environment, CFAC served as the primary permanent U.S. Naval presence in South Korea, acting as both a diplomatic post and a logistics station for incoming vessels. Despite its strategic importance, the medical facilities on the base were limited. “We had a very small dispensary with rudimentary capabilities,” said Dr. Frenning. “I feel like I was dealing with more than I should have been able to handle.” A typical day at the dispensary involved treating U.S. military personnel, Marines, and their families in the morning. In the afternoon, the dispensary opened its gates to the local Korean population to provide basic medical care. The Frennings departed South Korea in 1974 and returned to Minnesota where Dr. Frenning completed his residency at the University of Minnesota, specializing in oncology and hematology. He practiced medicine for 43 years until his retirement in 2020. In September 2026, Dr. Frenning and his wife, Carol, returned to South Korea through the Revisit Korea Program sponsored by the Republic of Korea’s Ministry of Patriots and Veterans Affairs. The program is designed to recognize the service of military personnel on the Korean peninsula and support the bilateral defense alliance. The program fully funds travel for eligible veterans and partially funds travel for one accompanying family member or caregiver. It is open to veterans of the Korean War, as well as personnel who served in Korea as members of the United Nations Forces or U.S. Forces Korea after the 1953 armistice. Organized with stateside support from the Korea Defense Veterans Association (KDVA) and the Korean War Veterans Association, the initiative allows participants to meet veterans from different eras of service and visit sites such as the Seoul National Cemetery and the War Memorial of Korea. The attendees were also able to visit nearby U.S. bases including Camp Humphreys and Osan Air Base. This 5-day itinerary allowed the veterans to truly see the impacts their service has made on both the Korean community and the alliance between the Republic of Korea and the U.S “They really emphasized how important it is to maintain this defense alliance, and I strongly support that,” said Dr. Frenning. Once completed with the official visit in Seoul, the Frennings were able to extend their trip and visit their old home in Chinhae, South Korea. During their visit, Dr. Frenning observed significant infrastructure changes, both in the region and at the military installation. Today, transportation to Chinhae is facilitated by multiple tunnels constructed through the surrounding mountains, which has improved regional access and eased medical evacuations. Furthermore, the base clinic now operates as a branch of the U.S. Naval Hospital Yokosuka in Japan, offering expanded services. “I think the upgrades are very important in the clinic area,” noted Dr. Frenning upon visiting the modernized facilities. “They have such good access to specialists when needed, and I didn’t have that much support.” The Frennings expressed thanks to the facilitators of the program for making it possible for them to revisit the place where they started their family. The Revisit Korea Program is open to all eligible veterans who served in Korea, and interested individuals are encouraged to apply through the Korean War Veterans Association.

items.title: Two Dover Airmen Sentenced in Multimillion-Dollar Cyber Fraud Scheme
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A federal judge recently sentenced one Airman and a former Airman to a combined 15 years in prison and ordered them to pay $1.36 million in restitution for a two-year cyber fraud scheme they perpetrated while serving on Active-Duty at Dover Air Force Base, Del. The post Two Dover Airmen Sentenced in Multimillion-Dollar Cyber Fraud Scheme appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
A federal judge recently sentenced one Airman and a former Airman to a combined 15 years in prison and ordered them to pay $1.36 million in restitution for a two-year cyber fraud scheme they perpetrated while serving on Active-Duty at Dover Air Force Base, Del.

On Sept. 25, Chijioke Timothy Odimegwu, 25, and Harafat Mogaji, 26, were sentenced to nine years, three months, and six years, six months in federal prison, respectively, for their role in a cyber fraud scheme that targeted at least 15 businesses, towns, and nonprofits while also conducting romance fraud schemes to get victims to act as “money mules” for their more than $2.4 million in stolen funds.

Neither man was involved in cyber career fields in the Air Force.

Odimegwu and Mogaji previously pleaded guilty to charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to commit access device fraud, and aggravated identity theft.

The Air Force Office of Special Investigations’ Detachment 306 at Dover assisted the FBI in the investigation. The detachment, a local field unit, helped identify victims, investigated threats made by the defendants, and conducted federal arrests of the two Airmen, according to an AFOSI release.

“This case demonstrates why strong partnerships across law enforcement are critical to protecting the Department of the Air Force and the American people,” said Special Agent Kevin Golden, commander of the detachment.

Mogaji was discharged from the USAF earlier this year; as of his recent sentencing, Odimegwu was still awaiting discharge.

Airman First Class Odimegwu joined the Air Force in February 2023, became a Traffic Management Apprentice, and last served as a household goods specialist, according to an Air Force spokesperson. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, and the Air Force Good Conduct Medal.

Mogaji served from 2022 to July 4, 2026. His terminal rank was Airman First Class; he was a services apprentice and last served as a fitness and sports journeyman. His awards include the Air Force Training Ribbon, the Global War on Terrorism Service Medal, the Air Force Outstanding Unit Award, the Air Force Good Conduct Medal, and the Air Force Longevity Service Award.

According to court documents, the pair spoofed the victims’ email addresses with similar addresses, gained username and password access to the victims’ accounts, and then monitored them for large financial transactions.

“Cyber-enabled crime does not stop at installation boundaries or geographic borders,” Golden said. “Working alongside our federal partners allows us to identify threats, protect our personnel and resources, and hold those responsible accountable.”

In one instance, the pair targeted a victim in Iowa City, Iowa, and were able to gain access to a $1.68 million wire transfer the nonprofit was using for a construction project and divert it to a Chicago bank account.

In another example, the pair phished an official from the City of Athens, Ohio, intercepted a $720,000 wire transfer, and used a romance scam victim as the money mule to take the initial transfer before moving it to their own accounts.

“The city has received $205,000 to date in recovered stolen funds and a $200,000 insurance payout,” Mayor Steve Patterson said at a Sept. 28 city council meeting.In late 2025, the city adopted a state-recommended cybersecurity policy that outlines specific procedures for electronic payments.

“Criminals from all backgrounds attack our digital systems. They strike targets from corporate networks to personal smartphones,” Eugene Kowel, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Omaha Field Office, said in a Department of Justice release. “No one and no device is immune from the threat. This case demonstrates that we will hold accountable cybercriminals who target our communities. It also serves as a reminder that every organization and every individual should take steps to protect their devices and systems and learn how to recognize and avoid scams.”

items.title: It’s official: US Army’s improved M8 rifle to begin fielding in December
items.author: Hope Hodge Seck
items.summary: The U.S. Army will begin fielding Sig Sauer’s M8 rifle in December, replacing the M7 with a lighter, shorter carbine based on soldier feedback.
items.body:
NEWINGTON, N.H. – On the factory floor at gun maker Sig Sauer’s headquarters, giant shipping pallets of the brand-new M8 Next Generation Squad Weapon rifle sit shrink-wrapped on shelves, ready for dispatch to soldiers.

Fielding of the M8 carbine, which appears set to replace Sig Sauer’s M7 as the Army’s standard rifle less than three years after the M7’s initial fielding began, will begin in December with some units at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, company executives confirmed to Military Times Monday.

The NGSW new weapons rollout also includes Sig’s M250 machine gun, which will replace the aging M249 Squad Automatic Weapon and is expected to reach troops in the first half of next year, said Dave Buehler, the company’s vice president of manufacturing.

Both weapons share an ammunition caliber: the 6.8×51mm Common Cartridge developed by Sig Sauer with a hybrid design intended to withstand high chamber pressure.

The M7 stumbled out of the gate, generating complaints from soldiers about its unwieldy weight and length and undue wear they said the high-pressure rounds were putting on components, including barrels and suppressors.

While Sig Sauer pushed back at the time on a number of the most strident complaints, the company is now casting the transition from the M7 to the M8, also previously called the XM8, as a success story that highlights its ability to act quickly on soldier inputs.

“From our perspective [the M8 is] a far superior rifle to the M7,” Buehler said. “On the M7, our hands were kind of tied [with what] the design criteria or characteristics of the contract required – even if we didn’t like them, we had to meet them. So now, the M8 considers our feedback, the soldiers’ feedback. And we can’t wait to get it out there.”

The new rifle is more than a pound lighter than the M7 and sports a barrel that’s 3.5 inches shorter. It replaces a less-popular folding stock with a fixed stock and includes feedback-based adjustments like added rigidity for the handguard. For soldiers who previously received the M7 rifle, the M8 should be a smooth transition, said Josh Shoemaker, Sig Sauer’s product manager for defense.

“The fundamentals are all the same, really,” Shoemaker told Military Times in an interview. “If guys that have had the M7 already are pretty familiar with that, the M8 will be a well-received transition.”

The foremost design challenge, he said, was achieving weight reduction from the M7, which weighed more than eight pounds unloaded, and nearly 10 pounds with the included suppressor – a radical difference from the legacy M4A1 carbine, which weighs 6.34 pounds unloaded.

Shoemaker said Sig Sauer had reduced the weight difference between the M4 and M8 to a little less than a pound, though that doesn’t include the M8’s suppressor.

“We worked really hard to reduce weight where we could and where it matters. So there’s lots of lightening cuts around the receiver. We pulled some weight out of the barrel, but we’re very careful to do that, because a lot of times when you pull weight out of the barrel, you have risks of some performance decreasing, whether that be barrel life or cook-off,” Shoemaker said. “We’re very sensitive to that, so it’s a long process to be able to figure out where your left and right limit is and how much weight [you can] kind of pull off of that before it’s too much.”

Reducing barrel size and thus altering the weapon’s center of gravity helped in that effort, Shoemaker said.

“When you pick up that M8, the balance of it feels a lot better, with that suppressor being on a shorter weapon system,” he added.

As for the M7, budget documents released earlier this year show the Army is curtailing its procurement, with none additional requested for Fiscal Year 2027 and about 50,000 previously delivered to the force.

The Army hasn’t said what it plans to do with the M7s already in inventory, particularly if it opts to put M8s in the hands of all troops who previously got the M7.

Shoemaker said there were “tons of options” for the Army with regard to M7s, including sending the weapons to basic training units or reassigning them to Guard or Reserve units.

But there’s another option, he said: the Army could ask for conversion kits to turn all the M7s already in its inventory into M8 carbines.

“The barrel is two screws that come out, and the hand guard is two more screws … the lower-end serialized item is the same,” he said. “All in, you could probably convert [an M7 to an M8] in under five minutes.”

If that’s an option Army leaders are considering, they have yet to address it publicly.

“There’re lots of options that the Army is well aware of,” Shoemaker said, “and making decisions on what direction they’ll go with that.”

items.title: Pentagon names 4 directed-energy weapons for counter-drone program at US bases
items.author: Michael Scanlon
items.summary: The Pentagon named four directed energy weapons for a homeland counter-drone program, the first systems to be fielded and tested at U.S. bases.
items.body:
The Pentagon on Monday named four directed-energy weapons for a homeland counter-drone pilot, the first systems the military will field and test at U.S. bases under a program ordered by Congress.

The four systems selected are AeroVironment’s Palletized High-Energy Laser, Epirus’ Leonidas high-powered microwave, Kord’s Firefly high-energy laser and Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon System, the Defense Department said in a release.

The pilot is run by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, or JIATF-401, the Army-led organization set up last year to coordinate counter-drone work across the military and other federal agencies.

“High-energy lasers and high-powered microwave systems are tools that can be effectively used in a layered drone defense,” Army Brig. Gen. Matt Ross, the task force director, said in the release. “This pilot program will test these capabilities in an operational environment so we can understand how best to integrate and sustain them to defend the homeland.”

The department said the pilot will gather real-time data on how the systems perform, what they cost and what it takes to operate and maintain them.

Ross said in August the pilot will run for a year, with service members operating and maintaining the weapons at the bases. The task force is coordinating the pilot with the services, U.S. Northern Command and the Federal Aviation Administration, or FAA.

In May, JIATF-401 selected five sites for the pilot: Fort Huachuca, Arizona, and Fort Bliss, Texas, both tied to the southern border mission; Naval Base Kitsap, Washington; Grand Forks Air Force Base, North Dakota; and Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri.

Officials said at the time that deployment plans would be worked out with installation commanders over 180 days, with operations expected later this year. Monday’s release does not say which system will go to which installation, how many of each will be fielded or what the systems and the pilot as a whole will cost.

Cost is the main selling point for lasers and microwaves, and one of the things the pilot is meant to test. Firing one costs a fraction of the price of a missile or even a gun round, and neither leaves unexploded ordnance on the ground.

Ross told reporters in August he was skeptical of per-shot math alone. “If I procure that system and it costs me $6 million and I take one shot a year, you can’t tell me that that shot only costs 8 cents,” he said.

Beyond cost, lasers and microwaves address different threats. A high-energy laser dwells on one drone at a time until it burns through. A high-powered microwave can thwart a swarm of drones in a single burst by overwhelming their electronics, though its wider footprint raises concern about effects on nearby systems.

Among the lasers, AeroVironment’s system is the company’s LOCUST laser in a roll-on, roll-off configuration, meaning it is packed onto a self-contained pallet that can be moved by truck or ship and set up wherever needed.

The company said in April that a palletized LOCUST tracked and defeated target drones aboard the aircraft carrier George H.W. Bush in an October 2025 live fire with the Navy and the Army’s rapid weapons development office.

In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million deal to produce its 30-kilowatt LOCUST X3 under the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, which the company called the first production contract for a U.S. directed-energy weapon. The Pentagon release does not say whether the pilot systems are drawn from that buy.

Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon System, or CLWS, is a lower-power laser. Lower power generally means a laser must remain on a target longer to destroy it, but the system itself can be smaller and easier to move.

Boeing said in 2024 that a 5-kilowatt CLWS defeated Group 3 drones, which can weigh up to about 1,320 pounds, at the Red Sands counter-drone exercise in Saudi Arabia, using targeting data from the Army’s Forward Area Air Defense network. At the time, the company said the system had defeated nearly 500 drones in testing and demonstrations at ranges from about 200 meters to 2.5 kilometers.

Boeing also said CLWS units had returned from a multiyear overseas deployment with the Marine Corps but did not say whether they engaged hostile drones.

Kord, a KBR subsidiary, markets Firefly as a palletized, mobile laser scalable from 5 to 40 kilowatts. Company officials told reporters at an August demonstration near Guntersville Dam in north Alabama that a truck-mounted version typically needs a few seconds on target to down a small drone.

Leonidas is the only microwave counter-drone system in the pilot. Built by Epirus, it is the basis for the Army’s prototype high-power microwave for defending troops and sites against drone swarms, part of the Indirect Fire Protection Capability program.

The Army awarded the company $66.1 million in December 2022 for four prototypes and another $43.5 million in July 2025 for a second-generation version.

Epirus said in September 2025 that a Leonidas disabled all 61 target drones across five scenarios at Camp Atterbury, Indiana, including a 49-drone swarm in one burst.

The pilot follows a rough start for lasers in domestic airspace. In February, the FAA briefly closed the airspace over El Paso, Texas, after a counter-drone laser was used near Fort Bliss without coordinating with the FAA, the Associated Press reported at the time.

To address safety concerns, defense and FAA officials held a live-fire demonstration in March at White Sands Missile Range, New Mexico. AeroVironment later said the system tested was its LOCUST laser, the same family as the palletized system named in Monday’s pilot announcement.

On April 10, the FAA said a safety review found that the laser systems tested, with proper safety controls in place, “do not pose undue risk to passenger aircraft.”

The department said it will continue evaluating other directed-energy technology and will host a shoot-off in December at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, for additional laser and microwave systems.

Ross, the task force director, said in August the shoot-off is being set up so systems that perform well “can immediately result in a purchase order that allows us to start building the production lines to get these systems into the field.”

The pilot is one piece of a greater, ongoing effort. On Sept. 29, the Army announced that JIATF-401 had awarded 10 contracts worth up to $4.15 billion combined for sensors, optical sights and gun-based systems to support Domestic Shield, the push to protect priority Defense Department sites within the United States.

Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

items.title: France fires upgraded nuclear-capable missile from submarine for first time
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday.
items.body:
PARIS — France test-fired an upgraded version of its M51 strategic ballistic missile from a submarine for the first time on Tuesday, a capability demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron called “very important” for the country’s strategic credibility and which he said would be monitored by allies and adversaries alike.

The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarine Le Vigilant fired an M51.3 missile in an acceptance test following the boat’s overhaul, the Ministry of the Armed Forces said in a statement. The missile, which didn’t carry a nuclear warhead, was launched off Finistère in western France and splashed down in the North Atlantic several hundred kilometers from any coastline, the ministry said.

France’s work to upgrade the M51 missile, manufactured by ArianeGroup, is part of a broader modernization of the country’s nuclear deterrence apparatus that also includes the construction of new ballistic-missile submarines and a future upgrade of the Rafale fighter jet that would carry a hypersonic nuclear cruise missile.

“This is a very important moment for our strategic credibility,” Macron told troops onboard a French Navy vessel from which he observed the launch. “Everything that has happened recently and what is happening today will be closely scrutinized by both our allies and our competitors alike, and it already is. Along the course we have set, this is a step forward.”

The modernization of France’s nuclear arsenal comes as the country works with several European allies on what Macron has called “forward deterrence,” a proposal that could involve extending the reach of French nuclear deterrence to those allies, although the details of what that would look like remain vague for now.

Every major overhaul of a French nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine is followed by an acceptance test firing of the M51, the ministry told Defense News in an emailed response to questions.

ArianeGroup and France’s Directorate General for Armament completed a first flight test of the modernized M51 from a launch site in Biscarrosse in southwest France in 2023, and the new missile entered operational service in October last year.

The latest M51.3 variant is estimated to have a range of more than 9,500 kilometers, from more than 9,000 kilometers for the previous version, according to the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. The missile carries four to six multiple independently-targetable reentry vehicles, or MIRVs, according to the Bulletin.

While the official range of the missile is undisclosed, ArianeGroup says the M51 reaches an altitude of more than 2,000 kilometers before reentering the atmosphere at a speed of Mach 20.

The missile is equipped with the new TNO-2 oceanic nuclear warhead, and offers better performance in terms of range, accuracy and penetration capability, according to the ministry. The solid-propellant three-stage missile weighs more than 50 metric tons, and each of France’s four ballistic missile submarines can carry 16 of them.

“The M51.3 ensures the long-term credibility of the ocean-based component in the face of evolving adversary missile defenses,” the ministry said. “It reflects the commitment of the President of the Republic to maintaining operational credibility of the nuclear forces over the long term, at the level required by the international environment.”

The first version of the M51 was fired from the Biscarrosse launch site in 2006, with the first submarine launch from the SSBN Le Terrible in January 2010. Today’s launch was the seventh time a variant of the M51 was fired from a French submarine, and the 13th launch of the missile overall, all of them “of course, conducted without a nuclear warhead,” according to the ministry.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: Northrop Grumman’s YFQ-48A CCA completes first fully autonomous flight
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: The successful flight came just weeks after U.S. Air Force officials announced their intention to have 500 autonomous aircraft in service by 2032.
items.body:
Northrop Grumman’s YFQ-48A Talon Blue Collaborative Combat Aircraft recently completed its first fully autonomous flight.

Talon Blue executed its first fully autonomous flight in Mojave, California, which included taxi, takeoff, in-flight maneuvers and landing, according to a recent company release.

The modular design, part of the defense company’s internally funded Project Talon portfolio, focuses on advancing manufacturing to lower cost and speed production without decreasing mission capability, per the statement.

Upgrades to manufacturing and design decreased part count and overall weight, which lowered the cost and increased the production timeline to meet the demand for autonomous systems.

“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness. We listened,” Craig Woolston, vice president and general manager of research and advanced design at Northrop Grumman, said in the release.

“Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities,” he continued. “Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”

The announcement came just weeks after U.S. Air Force officials announced their intention to have 500 autonomous aircraft in service by 2032.

Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink released the names of Anduril’s FQ-44A and General Atomics’s FQ-42A to be dubbed “Fury” and “Vengeance,” respectively. Production contracts for the two companies were awarded in June, a month before Anduril completed its first-ever live-fire test. General Atomics intends to have its live-fire testing this fall.

The Air Force has not awarded Northrop Grumman a contract for CCAs yet, but the company is included in the service’s baseline contract pool for mission autonomy software production.

The service chose six vendors in June for the software’s performance-based competition for Increment 1 with the aim of selecting one by summer 2027.

Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

items.title: Anduril, US Navy invest $6.6 billion to boost submarine parts production
items.author: Nathan Gomes and Shivansh Tiwary, Reuters
items.summary: Anduril will invest $3.7 billion to develop a new shipyard in Maryland to build critical components for the Navy’s Virginia-class submarines.
items.body:
Defense tech firm Anduril said on Tuesday it will invest $3.7 billion to develop a new shipyard in Maryland to build critical components for the U.S. Navy’s Virginia-class submarines, as Washington seeks to bolster its maritime defense capabilities.

Subsequently, the US Navy awarded Anduril a contract worth up to $2.9 billion to manufacture submarine components, with payments tied directly to production outcomes and the company assuming most of the execution risk, the defense startup said.

The investment and associated contract, together valued at up to $6.6 billion, come amid a broader push by the United States and its allies to expand arms production following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East.

The new plant, dubbed Arsenal-2, will be situated in Baltimore County and is expected to be up and running by the end of the decade, creating 3,100 direct jobs and supporting over 11,000 indirect jobs.

Asked about the $2.9 billion government contract, Christian Brose, chief strategy officer at Anduril, said, “It’s really the government buying the results of what we’re able to produce from the facility that we’ve invested in.”

Anduril is already building out a facility in California to manufacture critical Virginia-class submarine components such as torpedo tubes, helping address urgent capacity shortfalls in the U.S. industrial base, Brose said.

The company plans to expand into producing larger submarine modules and hull sections once its Baltimore shipyard becomes operational.

Virginia-class submarines, which can travel at over 25 knots, are the Navy’s latest generation of nuclear-powered attack submarines, designed for anti-submarine warfare, land-attack strikes and surveillance missions.

General Dynamics’ Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries jointly build the submarines.

Anduril, founded in 2017 by Palmer Luckey, is a defense firm that is best known for its autonomous systems, drones and software built for the U.S. military and its allies.

The startup has, however, expanded beyond drones into maritime and undersea systems and command-and-control software designed to connect military sensors, weapons and other systems.

The new plant comes after Anduril’s $1 billion Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio that began producing autonomous combat drones this year.

items.title: Guidance: Defence Employer Recognition Scheme
items.summary: The Employer Recognition Scheme (ERS) encourages employers to support defence and inspire other organisations to do the same.
items.body:
About the scheme

The Defence Employer Recognition Scheme ( ERS ) encourages employers to support defence and inspire others to do the same. The scheme encompasses Bronze, Silver and Gold awards for employer organisations that pledge, demonstrate or advocate support to defence and the armed forces community, and align their values with the Armed Forces Covenant .

The ERS is designed primarily to recognise private sector support although public sector organisations such as the emergency services, local authorities, NHS trusts and executive agencies are also eligible to be recognised.

Pledge your organisation’s support via the Bronze award or express your interest in applying for Silver or Gold award, contact us to find out more.

You can read our Privacy policy to find out more about how we process data.

Bronze award holders must have:

Signed the AFC and registered their interest for a Bronze award (via the ERS website).

Confirmed their understanding of the AFC and ERS and what it means to be a supporter of the Armed Forces community with the appointed DRM.

Informed their workforce of their positive support for the Armed Forces community.

Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:

How to develop a suitable HR framework to enable Reserve mobilisation for members of their work force.

Provide additional leave for Reservists (i.e. Part Time Volunteer Reserves) to conduct training.

How they would promote volunteering and support to the Cadet movement through official Cadet Force channels.

How they ensure that Service personnel/Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.

Nominate your organisation for a Bronze award

View the ERS Bronze award holders

Silver award holders in addition to Bronze Criteria must have:

ERS Bronze Award status and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be unusual for an organisation to achieve Silver status within 12 months of gaining Bronze.

Proactively demonstrate that Service personnel and Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.

Actively ensure that their workforce is aware of their positive policies towards the Armed Forces community. E.g. Internally publicised positive HR policy on Reserves in their workforce. In the case where no HR policy exists this should be demonstrated by specific references in job descriptions/organisation’s website.

Support Active Reservists (PTVRs) by:

Having Policy in place to support mobilisations or have made a commitment evidenced by their DRM that they understand the mobilisation process and would support a mobilisation if practicable. E.g. Employers of reservists must be aware of the role of Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) and how they support the Reservists in their work forces.

Demonstrated support to their training by providing at least 5 days additional annual leave (ideally paid).

A proactive relationship with their DRM, which can be demonstrated through various interactions, including but not limited to personal contact, automated communications, and engagement with supporting products or resources.

The employer must allow flexibility for employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers to fit their working hours in with their volunteering.

Scoping opportunities to support the Cadet movement (via official Cadet Force channels) through the following example activities: sponsorship, supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities; or providing employment advice and guidance.

Employ at least one individual from the Armed Forces community .

Hosting a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a local Reserve Unit or Military Command recruiting teams.

Have inclusive policy in place to support Strategic Reserves (those with an Ex-Regular and Callout liability).

View the 2026 ERS Silver Award Holders

Gold award holders in addition to Silver Criteria must have:Hold ERS Silver Award and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be very unusual for an organisation to achieve Gold status within 12 months of gaining Silver.

Be an exemplar within their sector, advocating for the AFC and or ERS to partner organisations, suppliers and customers with tangible positive results. E.g. demonstrate proactive steps/activity and clear success in encouraging partner organisations and their supply chain to engage with and sign the AFC, and or mentor others in progressing through the ERS .

Actively encourage a positive workplace environment for Active Reservists (Part Time Volunteer Reserves) by ensuring that positive policies in support of Reservists within the workforce are communicated to line managers and support their training by providing at least 10 days additional paid leave annually.

Demonstrate support to the Cadet movement by committing resources to improving the outcomes for cadets. This is to be achieved by verifying they deliver one or a combination of the following through official Cadet Force channels:

1) Sponsorship (e.g. for additional resources, competitions, events and specific activities such as overseas expeditions);

2) Supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities;

3) Providing employment advice and guidance.

Promote volunteering with the Cadet Forces by having policies in place that cater to offer additional paid or unpaid leave to employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers.

Engaged with CTP to support recruitment of Service leavers and have registered with the Forces Families Jobs website.

Support to Reserve Service and the wider Armed Forces community through internal and external communications, amplifying DRM social media messaging around Armed Forces Week, Reserves Day, ERS Gold /Silver announcements etc.

Actively finding out the numbers of Reservists employed and have a declared target for the number of Reservists within their workforce. Ideally, they will have relationships with the relevant Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) for reserve units in their local area.

If there are Reservists within the workforce, the employer has positively engaged with them on how the company would support their mobilisation.

Host a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a Reserve Unit or Military Command Recruiting Teams.

Where scale and business models permit, the employer should actively encourage and support an internal Armed Forces community network within their organisation.

View the 2026 ERS Gold award holders

Nomination and award process

Employers can sign up themselves for each award.

Nominations will be validated to determine the level of defence personnel employment within the nominated organisation and to check that the organisation has signed the Armed Forces Covenant .

Once the nomination has been validated it will be considered by a selection board at national level for gold awards and regional level for silver awards. The selection boards will be a panel chaired by a senior military officer and they will consider each nomination against the award criteria. Organisations selected for gold and silver awards will be formally notified in writing and invited to the relevant award event.

items.title: Lithuania says it would pay the cost if US establishes military base
items.author: Andrius Sytas, Reuters
items.summary: Lithuania is ready to pay the cost to set up a permanent U.S. military base if Washington should agree to establish one there, the prime minister said.
items.body:
VILNIUS — Lithuania is ready to pay the cost to set up a permanent U.S. military base if Washington should agree to establish one there, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said on Tuesday.

On Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump said he would consider Lithuania’s request for a permanent base: “They are friends of mine, they are great people, so we will certainly look at it.”

Lithuania, a member of the EU and NATO, borders Russia and Moscow’s close ally Belarus. The United States has kept an armored battalion of almost 1,000 troops there since 2019, in overlapping rotations, meaning the troops arrive and leave every few months.

Sinkevicius said he proposed turning this into a permanent presence at a meeting with Trump’s envoy John Coale last month in Vilnius.

“I’m glad that this idea is being taken seriously... This is a critically important guarantee of deterrence and security,” Sinkevicius wrote on Facebook.

“Our partners only need to make the political decision to permanently station troops, and Lithuania is ready to cover the costs involved.”

items.title: Healing Moral Injury Among Veterans
items.author: Kathryn P. Derose
items.summary: Moral injury is an important concern for U.S. military veterans, and a growing number of faith-based organizations seek to address it. This report describes 17 of these organizations, their approaches, and how their work relates to veteran care.
items.body:
A Landscape Analysis of Community Organizations Providing Faith-Based Support

ResearchPublished Oct 6, 2026

This research was made possible by the Epstein Family Foundation.

Moral injury, distress arising from experiences that violate deeply held moral beliefs and expectations, is an important concern for U.S. military veterans, and a growing number of faith-based organizations seek to address it. In this report, the authors conduct a landscape analysis, examining 17 such organizations—describing their characteristics, approaches to moral injury, and links to the broader veteran-support ecosystem.

Moral injury, the distress that can arise from experiences that violate deeply held moral beliefs and expectations, is an important concern for U.S. military veterans. In this report, the authors examine the landscape of U.S. community-based organizations that provide faith‑based or spiritually informed support for moral injury among military veterans. Drawing on a systematic scan of publicly available information and qualitative interviews with 19 representatives from 17 participating faith-based organizations (FBOs), the authors describe how these organizations conceptualize moral injury, the approaches they use to support veterans, and how their work intersects with the broader veteran-support ecosystem, including the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), religious congregations, and other religious or spiritual communities.

The study is descriptive. The authors summarize the evaluation and outcome information that organizations have published or provided, including a small number of peer-reviewed pre-post studies and organizational reports on reach and participant feedback. They did not collect data from veterans, independently verify organizational data, or evaluate program effectiveness. Additionally, because the authors describe the participating organizations rather than evaluate them, the recommendations reflect implications and considerations rather than endorsements of specific programs or models.

- Participating FBOs addressed dimensions of moral injury but often did so through distinctively faith- and community-based practices. Programs targeted concerns well documented in the moral injury literature, including guilt, shame, and forgiveness. However, FBOs often placed greater emphasis than typical clinical or VA models on forgiveness from God, flexible faith-based meaning-making, and a reconnection to a specific religious or spiritual community.

- FBOs combined multiple program components that have some support in the broader veteran-services literature, but this approach remains underevaluated. Peer facilitation, communal sharing, family inclusion, and other program components align with existing evidence to varying degrees. Yet the evidence base rarely examines these components as an integrated, faith-informed model for moral injury support.

- FBOs described addressing relational and community needs that formal care might not fully meet. Organizations framed healing as a long-term process supported through social ties, opportunities for veterans to give back, and reconnection to religious, spiritual, or community life. This emphasis on sustained belonging and reintegration could be relevant for veterans who are reluctant to engage with formal systems or whose moral injury involves disconnection from their faith, family, or community.

- FBOs may extend the veteran-support ecosystem, but their role remains informal and unevenly supported. Organizations generally viewed their work as complementary and sometimes as bridges to other supports. Collaboration was often locally driven, dependent on informal relationships, and absent of consistent processes for partnering with VA, while limited evaluation capacity and administrative burdens constrained FBOs’ ability to document outcomes.

- Researchers and funders could support pragmatic evaluation designs feasible for small community-based organizations; distinguish among types of FBOs, which differ in capacity, structure, and evaluation readiness; and pair validated measures with measures of forgiveness, meaning-making, spiritual struggle, belonging, and family functioning.

- Funders and policymakers could invest in organizational infrastructure—staffing, data systems, and evaluation expertise—alongside program delivery and support technical assistance intermediaries that help FBOs build capacity without displacing local trust.

- VA could clarify how coordination with community-based faith and spiritual supports currently occurs and identify which partnership and funding requirements are fixed and which are modifiable for small organizations with limited administrative capacity.

- FBOs could maintain flexible, noncoercive approaches to faith and spirituality that remain inclusive of nonreligious and spiritually unaffiliated veterans, clarify their scope of services and how veterans are connected to clinical care when needed, and build evaluation capacity as resources permit.

- Religious congregations could partner with FBOs on practical support, aftercare, and community reintegration, and build familiarity with moral injury and military culture.
