items.title: Boeing locks in 7-year deal to triple PAC-3 MSE seeker output
items.author: J.D. Simkins, Claire Barrett
items.summary: The agreement follows a framework deal that was announced in April. Production will span seven years and be completed at Boeing’s Huntsville facility.
items.body:
Boeing announced Monday that it formalized a seven-year contract supporting the Pentagon’s Acquisition Transformation Strategy, signing an approximately $14.7 billion “undefinitized” agreement with the Pentagon that allows the firm to triple its Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement.

“Early investment and a relentless focus on quality and execution have positioned us to now deliver seekers at unprecedented levels in the near-term, and we’re committed to building on that momentum,” Steve Parker, president and CEO of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a release. “Our Boeing teammates could not be prouder of the role they play in protecting U.S. and allied service members, civilians and critical infrastructure worldwide.”

The agreement follows the framework deal that was announced in April. Production will be spread over seven years, matching Lockheed Martin’s push to surge production on the PAC-3 MSE all-up round.

Lockheed in January announced a seven-year framework agreement to increase annual PAC-3 interceptor production from approximately 600 to 2,000.

Work on the seekers began immediately, the company announced in April, and will be completed at Boeing’s facility in Huntsville, Alabama.

Boeing’s PAC-3 seekers work by identifying, tracking and knocking out a range of threats, from ballistic missiles and hypersonics to hostile air platforms.

Once the seeker identifies the target, the highly maneuverable interceptor, which uses a two-pulse solid rocket motor, engages and eliminates threats via direct body-to-body contact.

Monday’s announcement, meanwhile, comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions, particularly those deployed by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, has come under increased scrutiny over the past eight months.

The announcement also follows a busy week for Boeing. Last Tuesday, the U.S. Navy selected the company to build its F/A-XX sixth-generation carrier-based fighter under a development contract worth more than $20 billion. The same day, the Air Force signed a $2.38 billion order for 22 more F-15EX Eagle II fighters.

Military Times reporter Michael Scanlon contributed to this report.

J.D. Simkins is Editor-in-Chief of Military Times and Defense News, and a Marine Corps veteran of the Iraq War.

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She holds a master's degree in military history from King's College, London, and is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

items.title: Has the Pentagon given up on AI polygraph analysis of loyalty?
items.author: Aliya Sternstein
items.summary: AI-aided scanning of speech patterns, vocal stress or facial expressions to read minds lacks scientific backing and will compound errors, critics argue.
items.body:
As of July, the Pentagon had been prepping artificial intelligence tools that analyze text, voices and faces to estimate staff trustworthiness, according to declassified presentation slides and prior Defense Department statements.

Now, Pentagon officials say that some of that AI is not part of the current revamp of the polygraph interview process, after Defense News asked for a response to concerns about the earlier statements and the slides.

On Wednesday, the Pentagon’s Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, or DCSA, which vets security clearance holders and applicants, said in an emailed statement that “active research and development” for the “Modernizing Polygraph” effort “does not incorporate generative super intelligence, also known as artificial intelligence,” that creates new content — such as emails, graphics or voiceovers.

Nor does the effort include “large language models,” meaning chatbots like ChatGPT and other programs trained on giant data sets to engage in human conversation, DCSA added.

And the research does not involve “facial action coding [of emotions], micro-expression analysis or vocal analyses,” the statement said. “While those technologies are not part of the effort,” DoD will “continue to monitor emerging scientific capabilities to evaluate their potential utility down the road.”

DCSA did not address other types of AI models that, according to the slides, researchers had been developing to scan spoken and written language for “deceptive speech” patterns.

Wednesday’s statement came after Defense News sought a response to criticisms from national security lawyers, scientists and AI auditors about AI’s ability to analyze deception — meaning not just to lie, but to do so knowingly and willfully.

They warned that AI-aided scanning of speech patterns, vocal stress or facial expressions to read minds lacks scientific backing, will compound errors and may violate civil liberties in a domain where few such rights exist.

Defense News chronicled their concerns and the Pentagon’s prior research and development of AI-aided lie-detection and emotion-estimation tools.

The recent DCSA statement, including the project name “Modernizing Polygraph,” contrasts with several earlier DoD statements, 2027 budget documents and DCSA slides that Defense News obtained through an open records request.

In July, a Pentagon official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the technology, explained the advantages of AI-driven sentiment and deception analysis.

“AI processes data in real time and enables standardized, objective data analysis,” the official told Defense News, via email. “AI-based analysis is a force multiplier for our human investigators, not a replacement.”

The official added, “The models are primarily trained on data from laboratory-controlled studies using volunteer participants.”

The DCSA slides, which include presentations from 2021 through 2025, show that the Air Force, DCSA and academic labs had been working on “sentiment analysis” AI models and “deceptive speech” AI-aided analysis since 2019, as part of a “Credibility Assessment Modernization” project.

In July, the DoD official described the AI models as part of a larger multi-year “transformation,” which the official referred to interchangeably as “Polygraph+” and Credibility Assessment Modernization.

Current budget materials price the Polygraph+/Polygraph Next project at $31 million, including costs for AI “scoring algorithms” and “decision aids,” thermal imaging tools to spot blood flow changes that can reflect stress and other non-contact sensors.

On Friday, DCSA declined to provide additional information, including the scope of the “Modernizing Polygraph” project and the decision not to include AI-based voice screening and facial expression analysis.

Trained on Twitter and Reddit

Over the summer, Farakh Zaman, a developmental leader at the Air Force Office of Scientific Research, elaborated on the appeal of AI-aided deception analysis.

“By processing subtle physiological, vocal and linguistic cues, these developmental algorithms may help establish a more objective baseline for investigators and pinpoint specific areas requiring further human-led clarification,” he said by email in July.

Wednesday’s DCSA statement said that the Air Force is not involved in the “active” research and development phase.

One undated declassified DCSA slide describes the Air Force amassing “deception-related” text to create a “deep learning model,” an algorithm that analyzes hordes of data to find patterns. The Air Force trained an early model on text from websites including Twitter, Reddit and other vocabulary data sets such as WordNet, according to the slide.

“This baseline training helps the algorithms understand natural, modern linguistic patterns, slang and everyday vocabulary,” Zaman explained in July. He acknowledged the need for “further rigorous testing, validation and a clear transition path” before fielding a prototype.

A separate DCSA slide, dated May 2025, contains a flowchart that depicts an avatar — a computer-generated image of an interviewer — in front of a security clearance applicant. Next to the applicant, a camera and microphone feed audio, video and speech-to-text data from the interview into various large language models. The recording devices and algorithms interact to gauge the applicant’s emotional state, while a human investigator observes and keys in questions for the avatar to ask.

DCSA’s Wednesday statement said the university that drafted the chart is not involved in the current research and development stage.

According to another undated DCSA slide, DoD has set a goal for natural language processing technology to interpret an interviewee’s feelings with 75% accuracy.

In July, the Pentagon official said by email that a human investigator remains essential for “the contextual reasoning and emotional intelligence required in these sensitive interviews.”

‘I’ve caught AI lying to me’

Ahead of Wednesday’s statement, Mark Zaid, a national security attorney who reviewed the slides, warned that the danger of derailing a military officer’s career is too great for AI to misinform an investigator.

The polygraph device “is just registering the physiology of the person,” such as spikes in breathing rate, perspiration or blood pressure, he said. “Then a human examiner analyzes those reactions to render an opinion.”

Here, however, “AI would be taking the polygraph readings and rendering an opinion” to the human examiner, said Zaid, who has represented individuals on all sides of the polygraph table, from workers disputing revoked clearances to former government officials and polygraphers.

“Now, we’re starting to get into the movie Minority Report,” he said, referencing a 2002 Steven Spielberg film that depicts a government reliant on psychic children for tips to predict crimes and detain people accused of future crimes.

Zaid, whose own clearance was revoked temporarily after he represented a whistleblower pivotal in President Trump’s first impeachment, said, “That concerns me more than the polygraph,” if science does not back AI’s reliability.

So far, scientific studies do not.

Rather, decades of research have discredited theories, popularized by shows such as Lie to Me, that anyone — human or artificial — can recognize deception based on speech patterns, vocal stress or facial movements.

Another concern scientists and auditors have is bias: the Justice Department has warned that using emotion-recognition algorithms to measure worker competency can discriminate against high performers with intellectual or developmental disabilities, who algorithms do not always understand.

Also, “automation bias,” the tendency to take AI’s advice without question even when conflicting information exists, may further erode the polygraph system’s reliability, technologists warned.

“[T]here is simply no consensus that polygraph evidence is reliable,” the Supreme Court declared in a 1998 decision banning polygraph results and polygraphers’ opinions from military courts.

Zaid said he appreciates the attempt to retool polygraph testing but wants proof that the planned approach is in fact an improvement.

“Anytime we might be able to scientifically advance the ability to determine truth, with accuracy, would generally be a good thing,” he said. But “the first thing that jumps out at me with AI is how often it is wrong…I’ve caught AI lying to me.”

Greg Rinckey, a former Army Judge Advocate General Corps officer who now provides security clearance representation, said that today’s “technology is so outdated, where they’re using tubes around people’s chests and blood pressure and sweat, so, any way that you can get a more reliable test for security clearances, especially counterintelligence investigations [into leaks], is a step up.”

That said, he questioned, “What is the research saying on how accurate it is?”

At present, research suggests the odds of AI-aided speech, voice or face analysis pegging a lie are about 50:50.

AI is ‘assuming dishonesty’

“There are no – reliable – diagnostic cues for deception detection, and I have yet to see any evidence, whether it is with humans or with artificial intelligence, that goes against that trend,” said David Markowitz, a Michigan State University professor who studies AI’s ability to understand human communication.

For instance, “the leakage idea — that these microfacial expressions will leak out from our awareness, signaling veracity or deceit — there’s very little evidence to support that, unfortunately,” he said.

Markowitz expressed doubts about AI-based deception analyses that claim an accuracy rate of 75% because “that is not how accurately humans do it, and often these systems are a big reflection of how humans do it.”

For example, he pointed to a recent experiment in which he prompted a Google Gemini AI model to examine audio and video of mock interrogations of accused cheaters in a trivia game, all of whom claimed innocence and some of whom were lying. Prior studies had asked humans to observe the same interrogations. DoD has entered into agreements to run a secure version of Gemini on unclassified and classified networks.

Markowitz said that his study, “The [in]efficacy of AI personas in deception detection experiments,” found Gemini was just as inaccurate as humans, both faring no better than chance, when prompted to distinguish fraudsters from truth-tellers.

What’s more, compared to humans, AI was more likely to wrongly accuse a trivia player of lying.

Markowitz gave one possible reason for AI’s systemic distrust of trivia players: The AI “is assuming that someone must have done something wrong because why else would they be questioned,” he said. “Anytime that someone is in an interview setting where they might be accused of something, a large language model is assuming dishonesty.”

Supreme Court: The jury is the lie detector

The consequences of a machine, whether a heart monitor or a voice screener, potentially bungling a credibility assessment can last a year or longer, said Zaid, the national security lawyer.

When officers who have successfully passed exams without issue suddenly fail their latest polygraph test, DoD typically puts them “in a corner with a dunce cap on for a year before officials will re-administer another exam,” he said. “You can’t get promoted. You can’t get certain assignments. And you can’t go overseas, which, to case officers, is death careerwise.”

Further, civil courts routinely dismiss complaints when employees claim that inaccurate results cost them their clearances. Nearly 40 years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the courts have no power over such national security matters.

Concerns about power imbalances and due process prompted the European Union to label AI-aided polygraph tools as “high risk” and place strict limits on law enforcement’s use of them.

Stateside, the Supreme Court, in forbidding polygraph evidence in military courts, noted that allowing it would meddle with the human’s role, or, as it were, the jury’s role, in determining credibility.

“A fundamental premise of our criminal trial system is that the jury is the lie detector,” Justice Clarence Thomas wrote in the Court’s 1998 United States v. Scheffer decision.

Pointing to the court’s decision, Zaid said that he wants assurances of due process when staff undergo administrative proceedings to contest a revoked clearance resulting from misaligned algorithms. Comparing the situation to successful cases disputing speeding tickets caused by a miscalibrated street camera, Zaid questioned, “Would the person be provided the evidence? An understanding of the AI’s training?”

Pentagon officials have long stressed the desire for AI-based lie detection to help curb gender and cultural biases that human investigators may carry into an interview room.

At the same time, employers’ use of similar technology for pre-employment screening has faced allegations of other biases and system errors.

“Facial expression analysis is heaviest in terms of biases against individuals with disabilities,” said Jo Ann Oravec, a University of Wisconsin professor whose research focuses on AI, public policy and disability issues.

For instance, AI-powered video screening of job applicants tends to misinterpret the involuntary twitches or vocal outbursts of skilled people with certain disabilities — and thus pass over qualified applicants, said Oravec, author of the 2024 article “From Polygraphs to Truth Machines: Artificial Intelligence in Lie Detection.”

In response to concerns about such biases in July, the Pentagon official said via email that the credibility assessment modernization plan adheres to DoD’s AI Ethical Principles of “responsible, equitable and traceable” use of algorithms.

The Air Force’s Zaman, in his July email, said that his team’s work aligns with DoD’s Responsible Artificial Intelligence Guidelines.

Researchers “are actively engineering and testing these models” to account for “diverse, representative training data,” he stated. The testing covers “broad variations in speech, language and expression.”

Ryan Carrier, founder of ForHumanity, a global nonprofit that helps organizations audit AI systems, said that the Pentagon’s principles and guidelines are a skeleton of those that the European Union follows and that ForHumanity uses for inspections.

For example, the EU’s AI Act demands users of high-risk systems receive training to overcome a different kind of bias called “automation bias” — or the tendency to execute AI’s advice without questioning its accuracy. This bad habit can lead to incorrect data overriding correct decisions, Carrier said.

Also, multimodal systems, meaning AI systems that simultaneously parse audio (the subject’s voice), video (their facial movements) and text (interview transcriptions), tend to misalign data and results, yielding an irrelevant analysis, Carrier said.

The system “could be making determinations that a person is lying or trying to deceive me that are outside of the tool’s specifications,” he explained.

In response to concerns about multimodal systems in July, the Pentagon official had said, “Any automated output is treated strictly as auxiliary data for a highly trained, certified polygraph examiner.”

Similarly, Zaman, at the time, said that investigators who use AI-aided deception-detection systems are “trained to contextualize the tool’s findings, preventing automated outputs from dictating an outcome.”

To safeguard against mismatched data or results, the Air Force keeps a documented history of each piece of data’s origin and modifications and brings in independent white-hat hackers to try producing false correlations, he added.

“We recognize that multimodal AI systems present unique technical challenges, and mitigating these risks by hardening our systems is central to our engineering and testing protocols,” Zaman said.

Reason for suspicion?

In August, when the Pentagon administered a raft of polygraph exams to probe leaks alleging the Iran conflict is depleting U.S. arsenals, some observers suspected the endgame was not to find the leakers, but to crack down on disloyalty.

Critics of the planned system said that AI-based deception analysis may be best suited to achieve the same purpose.

“If it’s purely an intimidation technique, it may not be utterly useless from the point of view of large bureaucracies,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst with the American Civil Liberties Union’s Speech, Privacy and Technology Project.

The expectations for AI-powered trustworthiness testing resemble the hope that U.S. national security officials held out for the polygraph about 100 years ago, other lawyers said.

Polygraph devices “were seen as this magic-miracle-machine when they first came out,” and, over time, the government learned that when seemingly making deductions, the tools were “actually just flagging correlating factors, like heart rate and physiological factors that can indicate lying, but aren’t actually reflective of it,” said Jake Laperruque, deputy director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s Security and Surveillance Project.

He added, “Thinking that AI sentiment analysis tools are actually making an assessment or engaged in reasoning — that’s not what those machines are actually able to do.”

Aliya Sternstein is an investigative journalist who covers technology, cognition and national security. She is also a research analyst at Georgetown Law. Her writing on the intersection of public health and constitutional rights has appeared in the Stanford Law Review, Arizona Law Review, and other law and health academic journals.

items.title: US Army tests counter-drone tech at Mexican border as cartel drone use rises
items.author: Mike Blake, Reuters
items.summary: The service is seeking to sharpen its defenses against the growing threat of drone use by cartels.
items.body:
The U.S. Army is testing counter-drone technology in the U.S.-Mexico border area, seeking to sharpen its defenses against the growing threat of drone use by cartels and emulate the rapid battlefield innovation happening in Ukraine’s war with Russia.

At Falcon Peak, a U.S. Northern Command exercise held in September in Arizona, soldiers watched as defense firms demonstrated radars, interceptor drones, autonomous gun systems and other technologies designed to detect, track and destroy small unmanned aircraft.

Army officials said drones crossing the southern border are typically systems sold commercially and used by criminals for surveillance linked to their smuggling and human trafficking operations. Brigadier General Brian Filler, deputy commander for operations at Joint Task Force Southern Border, told reporters the military detected 378 drone incursions in the previous 30 days and that the trend was increasing.

“We are seeing largely commercial off-the-shelf available drones,” Filler said, adding that most carry surveillance cameras and are often observed alongside cross-border movements.

The U.S. military said earlier this month it had downed 11 cartel drones using lasers since deploying the technology along the southern border in August.

Learning from Ukraine

Military planners are racing to keep pace with lessons from Ukraine, where drones have transformed the battlefield and driven rapid innovation in both offensive and defensive systems.

Military officials caution that cartel-operated drones are not comparable to the sophisticated battlefield ones seen in Ukraine or the Middle East. But they say the border offers a valuable operational environment to test equipment, train soldiers and evaluate how systems perform outside controlled laboratory conditions.

The exercise highlighted the Pentagon’s growing embrace of venture-backed defense technology firms. Since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, investors have poured billions of dollars into companies such as Anduril, Shield AI, Saronic and a wave of smaller drone and counter-drone startups seeking military contracts.

Anduril’s Ghost drone was featured in the demonstrations, as well as the radar-and-camera detection system produced by Teledyne FLIR, the “Bullfrog” counter-drone automated machine gun produced by Allen Control Systems and an interceptor drone sold by Powerus, which went public on Thursday, merging with a company backed by sons of US President Donald Trump.

Officials said part of their goal is replicating the rapid iteration cycle seen in Ukraine.

“We tend to look at Ukraine and we say, ‘I am so impressed with how quickly they can adapt on a daily or weekly basis,’” Brigadier General Matt Ross told reporters.

“What we should really do is replicate that process.”

items.title: European defense startups to raise record $10.5 billion in 2026, Dealroom forecasts
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: “This is Europe catching up rather than the U.S. slowing,” Dealroom said of the trend. “EU 27 funding more than doubled in a year.”
items.body:
PARIS — European defense startups are forecast to raise a record $10.5 billion of funding this year, roughly four times the $2.6 billion raised a year earlier and led by investments in firms developing drone technology, according to Dealroom, which tracks data on venture capital funding.

Defense startup funding in Europe already reached $7.4 billion as of Sept. 20, led by so-called “mega rounds” raised by Germany’s Helsing and Quantum systems, Dealroom and Resilience Media said in their annual State of Defence Tech report published Monday. That compares to $1.5 billion of funding for European startups in the defense space as of September a year earlier, based on the 2025 report.

Europe is grabbing a growing share of the defense-tech investment pie, with the European Union accounting for 21% of defense startup funding raised by September, from 15% last year. The share of the United States fell to 75%, the lowest ever, according to the Dealroom data.

“This is Europe catching up rather than the U.S. slowing,” Dealroom said. “EU 27 funding more than doubled in a year.”

Mega rounds made up more than 85% of the venture capital invested in European defense startups this year, including Helsing’s $1.8 billion Series E round in July according to Dealroom. German startups have set every fundraising record in European defense-tech venture capital funding since 2023, the report said.

Across NATO countries, defense startups raised $27.1 billion in venture capital so far in 2026, already more than $14.5 billion raised in all of 2025, and the amount is forecast to total $38.5 billion by the end of December.

Europe is channeling the largest share of venture capital into drones and autonomous systems, which accounted for 74% of the funding in the EU and 77% in the United Kingdom, compared to 57% in the United States. European startups in that segment that raised money included Helsing, Quantum Systems and Stark in Germany, Harmattan AI in France and Cambridge Aerospace in the U.K.

In Europe, the segment of unmanned aerial vehicles accounted for $4.7 billion raised as of September, according to the Dealroom data, followed by Earth observation and satellite imagery with $1.8 billion, anti-drone solutions and launch vehicles, each with $1.2 billion, and maritime robotics, with $796 million raised.

European startups in ground robotics, or unmanned ground vehicles, are trailing for now, with $77.6 million of venture capital funding so far this year, according to the Dealroom data.

Germany is the top European country for defense venture capital funding this year, with $3.5 billion raised, ahead of Finland with $1.2 billion, the U.K. with $932 million and France with $376 million. Munich is the European defense tech capital, attracting $3 billion in VC funding as of Sept. 20, ahead of Helsinki, London, Berlin, the English city of Cambridge, and Paris.

“Munich is the powerhouse of the European defense tech ecosystem,” Dealroom said. “Helsing and Quantum Systems drive most of it, together worth $25.7 billion. Behind them a younger cohort is forming across ground robotics, counter-drone and hypersonics.”

Funding for defense startups is diversifying as the sector grows, and total private investment in NATO defense startups, which also includes private equity, debt and grants, is forecast to reach $42.7 billion from $16.9 billion a year earlier, according to Dealroom.

Defense is the fastest-growing sector in Europe in terms of startup funding, ahead of space and robotics, according to Dealroom. Defense accounted for 15% of overall venture capital funding in the EU, from 6.2% reported a year earlier, while across NATO, defense attracted 4.9% of venture-capital funding as of September.

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: Germany to set up first drone regiment next year, modeled after Ukraine war lessons
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: Germany plans to stand up its first dedicated drone regiment next year, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced.
items.body:
VIENNA — Germany plans to stand up its first dedicated drone regiment next year, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced, as Berlin attempts to institutionalize lessons from the war in Ukraine after years of domestic foot-dragging on unmanned warfare.

Speaking Oct. 1 at the Bergen military training area during the army’s “Experimentalserie Land” trials, Pistorius said ground forces will begin forming the regiment in 2027. Officials credited direct operational exchanges with Ukrainian frontline units for shaping the live-fire trials, which tested both aerial drones and unmanned ground systems. Pistorius emphasized that ground robotics will serve as an equal operational pillar alongside aerial systems, with the regiment consolidating reconnaissance, deep-strike capabilities, unmanned ground vehicles, electronic warfare, and counter-drone defenses under a unified command.

The regiment will serve as a divisional asset assigned to the 10th Panzer Division − the formation earmarked as Germany’s high-readiness “Division 2025” pledge to NATO, which also oversees Panzerbrigade 45 in Lithuania.

German Army Chief Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding said the Bundeswehr is pursuing a dual-track strategy that envisions setting aside dedication formations while also institutionalizing drone usage throughout the entire force.. At the turn of the year, the service will simultaneously begin fielding tactical unmanned systems directly across three core combat branches: light infantry, reconnaissance, and armor units.

The army plans to recruit between 300 and 350 personnel for the regiment’s initial footprint in 2027 before expanding the unit to an end strength of up to 600 troops, according to Freuding. In remarks to German wire service dpa, Freuding said planners target full operational capability by 2029.

The envisioned structure comprises five or six companies, including units for close-range combat, deep strikes at ranges of up to 500 kilometers depending on commercial equipment availability, electronic warfare, counter-UAS protection, and an internal trials company intended to fast-track operational testing. The Bundeswehr also plans to equip the formation with loitering munitions, which are currently undergoing evaluation and should reach troops in 2027, according to dpa information.

Unmanned systems have fundamentally reshaped modern combat, accounting for the vast majority of casualties on the battlefield in Ukraine. Western militaries have often lagged in retrofitting their forces, slowed by peacetime procurement practices and protracted political debates over weaponized drones and autonomy.

Key procurement questions surrounding the new unmanned-tech formation remain. The defense ministry has yet to finalize a permanent basing location or award contracts for the specific long-range platforms the regiment requires.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: US Marine Corps anti-ship weaponry to see exercise action on remote Japan island near Taiwan
items.author: Leilani Chavez
items.summary: The U.S. Marine Corps will deploy its ground-based anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s southwesternmost island for exercises this month.
items.body:
MANILA, Philippines — The U.S. Marine Corps will deploy its ground-based anti-ship and air-defense systems to Japan’s southwesternmost island for exercise Keen Sword, placing new U.S.-Japan capabilities on an island sitting just 110 kilometers from Taiwan.

Keen Sword, the largest U.S.-Japan biennial joint drill, will feature two key systems of the Marine Corps’ littoral force: the anti-ship NMESIS (Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System) and air-defense MADIS (Marine Air Defense Integrated System).

Yonaguni’s local government disclosed the deployment on Friday, a day after the Okinawa Defense Bureau relayed deployment plans on Oct. 1.

The systems will be deployed to Yonaguni for the first time, as this year’s iteration shifts to ground-based, multi-island, sea-denial operations aimed at distributing American and Japanese forces across the southwestern islands.

The deployment also reflects a broader shift by the United States and Japan toward mobile missile and air-defense systems that can operate from scattered islands.

NMESIS and MADIS form the cornerstone of the U.S. Marine Corps’ force design modernization and restructuring plan, which moves away from heavy armored platforms to focus on small-unit, expeditionary forces that can capture and defend islands.

NMESIS can strike targets at around 115 miles and could threaten ships operating in waters around Taiwan. The reported deployment, in turn, has drawn criticism from Chinese military experts even while China’s PLA Navy and coast guard vessels have increased activities around Taiwan.

The NMESIS and MADIS systems first arrived with the Okinawa-based 12th Marine Littoral Regiment 3rd Marine Division in June. The units were earlier deployed to the Philippines’ northern Batanes Islands and western Laoag province during the Balikatan drills.

The deployment comes as Japan tests what defense officials describe as standoff-strike capabilities, missile systems that can strike targets far from enemy weapons, while strengthening its southwestern islands for distributed military operations.

According to the Ministry of Defense, troops from nine countries, including the Australian and French armies, will join 45,000 Japanese Self-Defense Forces personnel for this year’s exercise, which will run from Oct. 19 to 29.

The exercise will also bring together a number of U.S. and Japanese ground-based missile systems.

The U.S. Army will deploy HIMARS (High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems) weapons to Camp Ishigaki, some 80 miles from Yonaguni.

The Army’s Typhon missile launcher will also be moved to Okinawa mid-month, although no disclosures have been made about whether the mid-range system will be used for the exercise.

In past iterations of the drill, the USS George Washington joined the exercises, but the carrier strike group was sent to the Arabian Sea in August to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, which was returning home after a prolonged deployment.

That prominent naval absence is expected to emphasize the exercise scenario shift toward a land-based network of mobile systems.

Last year, exercises in Yonaguni focused on maximizing the island as a forward operating base. This year, Keen Sword will showcase the Ground Self-Defense Force’s three anti-ship missile systems, which are the core of Japan’s long-range standoff-strike capabilities.

The JGSDF will train with the new ground-launched Type-25 surface-to-ship guided missile system, formerly known as the upgraded Type-12, which was fielded across the Nansei Islands in late March. The Type-25 SSM has a strike reach of 1,000 kilometers.

The lineup also includes the Type-88 ground-to-ship missile and the upgraded Type 03 Chu-SAM Kai medium-range ground-to-air guided missile.

Keen Sword was originally planned as a much larger exercise, local government officials said, but opposition forced the ministry to scale it down to its current iteration.

Yonaguni is Japan’s last inhabited island in the Nansei, a chain of scattered islands in southwestern Okinawa and a fast-emerging flashpoint amid rising tensions around Taiwan.

The JGSDF set up a radar and surveillance system on the island in 2016 to fill a “surveillance vacuum” in the seascapes stretching from the island to Taiwan, according to officials.

The island has seen increased joint exercises between Japanese and U.S. troops while it faces incursions from Chinese ships.

In June this year, the government reported incursions by Chinese Coast Guard ships encroaching on Japan’s exclusive economic zone between Yonaguni and Taiwan. In 2022, China’s ballistic missile landed just 80 kilometers from the island.

While tensions surround the island, local officials have raised concerns about the use of civilian roads, ports, and airways.

Large equipment for the exercise will be transported by sea through Kubura Port, and local authorities have asked residents to avoid using roads during the movement of military equipment.

There are also concerns after a Japan Self-Defense Forces V-22 Osprey was involved in a ground-strike incident in the same exercise in 2024. The incident prompted then-defense minister Gen Nakatani to order the grounding of Japan’s 17 Osprey aircraft.

This year, however, the V-22 Osprey will not participate, Yonaguni Mayor Tsuneo Uechi told Mainichi Shimbun on Oct. 2.

While the island understands the need for military training, Uechi said it is not ready for large-scale exercises that exceed the island’s capacity. The local government remains opposed to the exercises and continues to hold talks with the defense ministry.

Leilani Chavez is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. Her reporting expertise is in East Asian politics, development projects, environmental issues and security.

items.title: Missiles, satellites and warplanes — Ukraine, Europe advance key arms projects
items.author: Jaroslaw Adamowski
items.summary: Ukraine’s Fire Point said the firm is developing an extended-range tactical ballistic missile after its FP-7 weapon was used in combat for the first time.
items.body:
WARSAW, Poland — Ukraine’s drone and missile maker Fire Point is developing an extended-range tactical ballistic missile after its FP-7 weapon was used in combat for the first time on Oct. 1, the company’s CEO Iryna Terekh said during this year’s Helsinki Security Forum.

As European nations are bracing for intensified Russian hybrid attacks, defense companies are pitching products for different capability gaps, with European and American producers partnering rather than working in isolation, industry representatives said during the event over the weekend.

Fire Point has developed its flagship missile, which has attracted praise from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to be part of the pan-European Freyja anti-ballistic missile defense program, with the system’s prototype expected to be ready in the first half of 2027. Meanwhile, the company is working on an extended-range version that is to be released this year, Terekh said during a panel discussion on the first day of the forum, Oct. 2.

“Yesterday we launched our ballistic missile onto Russian territory for the first time. It is a tactical ballistic missile for [a range of] 300 kilometers maximum. We are working on a longer [range] version that will also come this year,” Terekh said. “We were able to make this missile in two years as a private company.”

Fire Point’s executive said the capability is crucial for Ukraine, as the country is joining “a VIP league of operators of their own independent ballistic missiles with no kill switch. We don’t have to ask now anybody if we want to conduct self-defense.”

The Ukrainian authorities have entrusted a private company with developing a key component of the missile defense program because Fire Point has slashed bureaucracy and accelerated research and development on its missile range, she said.

“Also, we were able to make it a few times cheaper than any” competitor, Terekh said.

The forum was officially inaugurated by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Moldovan President Maia Sandu. Encouraged by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland joined NATO in April 2023. In Moldova, concern over intensifying Russian hybrid threats and the war in neighboring Ukraine is pushing the country’s government to seek closer cooperation with NATO, while maintaining its constitutionally mandated neutrality.

“This year, Russian drones have entered our airspace more than 45 times, eight of them in the past week. Last month, Russia deliberately hit Ukraine’s border crossings with Moldova, killing two people,” Sandu said during an Oct. 2 joint press conference with Stubb. “Our answer is to grow stronger. We are investing in air defense, modernizing our Army and raising defense spending.”

During the panel discussion featuring both heads of state, the Finnish president said that Russia has embarked on a campaign of hybrid warfare directed against Europe whose aim is to destabilize allied nations and “make sure we don’t support Ukraine.”

“The warfare that Russia is conducting in Ukraine is kinetic, traditional warfare. But what it is conducting in Europe is hybrid, and hybrid has many different elements. You have daily cyber attacks, you have sabotage attempts as we saw in Leipzig,” Stubb said.

Meanwhile, on Oct. 1, two Finnish companies, satellite operator Iceye and telecoms equipment giant Nokia, unveiled their new partnership to develop sovereign satellite communications for governments and defense customers, offering broadband low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications systems. The first satellites are to be launched in 2028.

Iceye is already supplying radar-satellite systems to numerous European allies, including Finland, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal and Sweden, and Germany’s December 2025 order for a 40-satellite constellation marked the first-ever European move to create a large tactical system on the continent, according to its CEO Rafal Modrzewski.

Modrzewski and Nokia’s CEO Justin Hotard discussed their companies’ joint project during a panel discussion at the forum, saying it comes in response to nations’ drive for sovereignty in satellite communications across priority mission areas.

“Sovereignty doesn’t exist without competitiveness. Sovereignty without competitiveness is isolation … and the reality, as we see here in Finland and in Europe is that neither the U.S., nor Europe can win in a war of isolation,” Hotard said.

Also on Oct. 1, Finland formally presented the first two of the 64 F-35 fighter jets the nation has ordered from Lockheed Martin. At a Helsinki Security Forum panel, Elizabeth Parcella, the vice president for Strategy and Business Development for Aeronautics at Lockheed Martin, said that, while the move improves Finland’s defense posture, it also comes as the company is expanding its manufacturing collaboration with local industry partners.

“Patria is a key partner with us. They are starting to manufacture the forward fuselage of the aircraft. They are also partnered with our engine provider, Pratt & Whitney,” Parcella said. “And, together with other European manufacturers, about 25 percent of the value of every F-35 will be produced in Europe moving forward.”

In his remarks during a panel, Panu Routila, the CEO of Patria, referred to last week’s award of a contract to supply the first Trackx light armored personnel carriers to Finland and Sweden as an example of how European nations work together to fill their capability gaps.

One example “is Trackx, our tracked vehicle, which we started developing just three years ago, actually, because of the demand for Arctic mobility, mobility in very difficult conditions. And this is a vehicle that is now ready,” Routila said.

Deliveries of the vehicles are to commence in 2027, Patria said in a statement.

“Following delivery, both countries will conduct national field trials and evaluations to assess the vehicles’ suitability for operational use. In addition, part of the testing is expected to be conducted jointly between the nations,” the statement said.

Jaroslaw Adamowski is the Poland correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: The Impact of Early Colleges on Postsecondary Performance and Completion
items.author: Christine Mulhern
items.summary: This article updates findings from a 17-year longitudinal experimental study on early colleges, examining the impact on postsecondary performance and completion.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Oct 5, 2026Published in: AERA Open, Volume 10, No. 1, pages 1-19 (2024). DOI: 10.1177/23328584241290772

Early colleges are a model of schooling that combines the high school and college experiences, providing students the opportunity to simultaneously earn a high school diploma and an associate degree or 2 years of college credit. This article updates findings from a 17-year longitudinal experimental study of the model, examining the impact of the model on postsecondary performance and completion. The study found positive impacts on overall degree completion, with very large impacts on associate degree completion. There were also positive impacts on bachelor’s degree completion for low-income students and first-generation college-goers. For students who enrolled in a public 4-year institution, the study found positive impacts on advanced coursetaking. There was no difference between treatment and comparison students on final college GPA or on the percentage of students who double-majored. Treatment students who earned a bachelor’s degree did so more quickly than comparison students.

items.title: Governing The Accelerator
items.author: Dean Ball
items.summary: This perspective examines how federally funded research and development centers can close gaps across three domains: data and infrastructure, algorithmic intelligence, and autonomous experimentation.
items.body:
The Case for National Collaboration in AI-Enabled Materials Discovery

Expert InsightsPosted on rand.org Oct 5, 2026Published in: Advanced Materials Technologies, e71315 (2026). DOI: 10.1002/admt.71315

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping materials discovery into a more integrated pipeline by combining data generation, surrogate prediction, and, in selected settings, closed-loop experimentation at an unprecedented rate. However, the institutional mechanisms needed to govern reproducibility, interoperability, and oversight across these workflows remain underdeveloped. This perspective examines how federally funded research and development centers (FFRDCs) can close that gap across three domains: data and infrastructure, algorithmic intelligence, and autonomous experimentation. In each, absent a national coordinating body, these decisions default to institutions not built for coordination, accountability, or mission persistence. We propose a two-tier leadership model in which science and technology (S&T) laboratories drive technical capability, while study and analysis (S&A) centers provide policy integration, cost-benefit analysis, and governance frameworks to translate scientific output into national strategy. Without a coordinating framework, the United States risks advancing a technology faster than it can govern it. Meanwhile, foreign competitors pursue centralized national materials programs of their own.

items.title: Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
items.summary: The annual Sanctuary Awards recognise outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the Ministry of Defence (MOD) estate.
items.body:
The Sanctuary Awards have been recognising outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the MOD estate since 1991.

The awards celebrate and encourage group and individual efforts that benefit sustainable development, environmental and heritage conservation, utilities and resource-saving measures, sustainable construction and procurement or community awareness on land or property that the MOD owns or uses in the UK and overseas.

35 th Sanctuary Awards 2026: Shortlisted entries

Winners will be announced on 17 November 2026. You can sign up for the free Sanctuary Awards 2026 live feed online.

Many congratulations to the 14 projects that have been shortlisted for the 35 th Sanctuary Awards 2026:

507 Specialist Team Royal Engineers – A1 Steam trust, Darlington Railhead Construction Project (A1 Steam Locomotive Trust, Darlington)

AA Wick Marsh Ranges (AA (Wick Marsh) Ranges, Fingringhoe, Colchester)

Aldershot’s Training Area – sustaining military capability (Aldershot Military Fieldcraft Training Areas)

Barton Stacey Flyfishing Club (Barton Stacey Training Area)

Beckingham Cadet Training Centre – sustainable construction (Army HQ, Andover)

Devonport Open Days (HMNB Devonport)

Group Captain Maurice Dixon (RAF Leeming and RAF High Wycombe)

Sq Ldr Don Earl (RAF High Wycombe)

Exercise Druid Sacrifice (RAF Valley)

Find it in Plymouth – supply chain resilience at Devonport (HMNB Devonport)

FuelActive – cleaner fuel for Team Leidos’ fleet (Defence Fulfilment Centre, DM Beith, MOD Bicester, JHC FS Aldergrove, MOD Kineton, MOD Longtown, DM Gosport, HMNB Portsmouth)

Lydd Ranges Sea Defence Project (Lydd Ranges)

Project Life (National Armaments Director Group Bicester)

SPINNERET – microgrids for operational energy ( MOD Bovington Camp)

Nominations were sought in the following categories:

Climate Change Resilience Award – projects or activities focused on taking action to enhance climate resilience through adaption.

Energy Award – for energy of fuel projects that decrease energy demand, increase energy efficiency and/or increase energy resilience through sustainability.

Environmental Enhancement Award – projects focused on wildlife, biodiversity, environmental research, or tackling pollution or contamination issues.

Heritage Award – projects focused on archaeology, historic buildings, historic parks or gardens, landscape preservation, museum collections, or heritage education or public engagement.

Individual Achievement Award – any individual who has made a significant personal contribution to MOD ’s sustainability or conservation ambitions.

Social Impact Award – grass-roots sustainability projects focusing on community engagement, green spaces, wellbeing or facilitating public access.

Sustainability Improvement Award – for projects that demonstrate sustainability improvements through implementation of circular economy principles (including reducing resource consumption or waste and recycling), sustainable procurement, sustainable construction or refurbishment projects, and improvements in equipment or systems through eco design.

The Operational Capability Award will be chosen from the shortlisted nominations and awarded to the project which best delivers enhanced operational capability through sustainability and climate considerations.

And the Silver Otter Trophy will be chosen from the category winners and awarded to the best Establishment, Conservation Group or community led project or individual conservation effort on the MOD estate.

items.title: Primary Care Physician Organization Affiliations With Health Systems Between 2014 and 2019 Were Associated With Modest Improvements in Quality of Care
items.author: José J. Escarce
items.summary: We examined whether affiliation of primary care physician organizations with vertically-integrated health systems improved quality of care or service utilization for Original Medicare enrollees and for PO groups expected to benefit from affiliation.
items.body: We examined whether affiliation of independent primary care physician organizations (POs) with vertically-integrated health systems improved quality of care or service utilization for Original Medicare enrollees overall and for groups of POs expected to benefit from affiliation. Using national Medicare claims, Provider Enrollment, Chain, and Ownership System (PECOS), and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 990 data from 2013 to 2019, we estimated changes in 13 quality and utilization measures following affiliation. We found that affiliation was not consistently associated with meaningful improvements in preventive care, chronic disease management, or utilization. Modest gains were observed in diabetic eye exams and organization-level care continuity, whereas primary care visits and specialist visits declined. Small POs exhibited additional gains in breast cancer screening relative to large POs, while low-quality POs and rural POs experienced lower relative performance on at least one other measure. These results suggest that health system affiliation alone does not yield broad improvements in quality across diverse types of primary care POs.

items.title: The Emerging Digital Battleground
items.author: Christian Trotti
items.summary: Digital infrastructure is now central to the U.S.-China rivalry. The authors identify nine factors that shape competition in global markets and offer five strategic priorities for the United States.
items.body:
Cost, bundled ecosystems, and on-the-ground presence give China structural advantages in the global digital network competition—but the United States can still catch up.

The digital networks connecting the world—fiber-optic cables, 5G systems, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, and space-based systems—are becoming the commanding heights of 21st-century geopolitics. Nations that shape this infrastructure will gain outsize influence over economic growth, security relationships, and governance norms.

China has pursued that influence aggressively through its Digital Silk Road, a component of the Belt and Road Initiative. The United States, meanwhile, lacks a coherent, well-resourced strategy to respond. RAND researchers used case studies, domain analyses, and interviews with U.S. government officials and private-sector leaders to identify what determines who wins this competition.

China’s bundled ecosystem is its sharpest competitive weapon.

- China’s leading advantage isn’t any single technology but its ability to combine hardware, software, financing, training, and diplomacy into turnkey packages that individual Western firms struggle to match.

Cost and financing drive adoption decisions in developing countries.

- Across every domain examined, financing was the most consistently cited factor in third-country procurement choices. In 2023, China’s export credit financing totaled $39 billion, versus the United States’ $2.7 billion.

The United States retains real advantages, but time is short.

- U.S. and allied firms lead in AI, subsea cables, cloud computing, and space launch. However, China is investing heavily to catch up. Third-country decisions could lock in dependencies for decades.

Most countries hedge rather than choose sides.

- Few nations align exclusively with either ecosystem. They mix Chinese hardware with Western software and court both sides, potentially allowing China to accumulate influence without achieving outright dominance.

Develop a national strategy and coordinating office:

- Create a single empowered body to align public and private efforts and replace the fragmented, agency-siloed approach.

Close the financing gap:

- Establish dedicated digital network financing programs that match China’s concessional terms as closely as possible.

- Where single-country terms cannot match Chinese offers, pursue pooled allied financing.

- Coordinate a U.S.–European Union–Japan approach that pools resources, shares technology offerings, and presents unified financing packages to multiply U.S. competitive capacity.

- Embed a cadre of digital service officers in key partner countries to support contract wins, train local workforces on Western platforms, and cultivate long-term relationships.

- Establish and maintain a coalition of countries committed to open, interoperable, and secure digital standards, without demanding the exclusivity that most hedging states will refuse.

RAND researchers used four complementary lines of analysis. They reviewed publicly available literature on digital network competition and China’s Digital Silk Road; conducted in-depth assessments of four priority domains—physical connectivity and infrastructure, wireless and Internet of Things networks and standards, AI infrastructure and data ecosystems, and space systems; built five original case studies examining digital network competition in Costa Rica, Nigeria, the Philippines, and Serbia and in the subsea cable sector; and conducted roughly a dozen interviews with current and former U.S. government officials and private-sector leaders with direct experience in digital network competition.

items.title: Inpatient Hospital Upcoding in California Among Fully Insured Commercial and Medicare Advantage Stays Between 2018 and 2023
items.author: Virginia Zhang
items.summary: In this report, the authors analyze Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group upcoding trends in California hospitals, finding that upcoding increased payments for commercial stays and raised out-of-pocket costs for some Medicare Advantage patients.
items.body:
ResearchPublished Oct 5, 2026

This research was sponsored by the California Health Care Foundation.

The authors examine inpatient hospital upcoding, using data from California’s Health Care Payments Database. Findings show that upcoding contributed to up to $554 million in higher payments to hospitals for commercial stays in 2023, compared with 2018 payments. Upcoding was concentrated in a few high-volume Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Groups and likely increased out-of-pocket spending for some Medicare Advantage patients.

items.title: Infinite Potential—Insights On Artificial Intelligence Loss of Control Across Five Scenarios
items.author: Barry Wilson
items.summary: The authors analyze observations from Infinite Potential games with AI loss of control to identify issues, capabilities, and recommendations needed to navigate the potential collapse of social legitimacy, economic stability, and technical control.
items.body:
RAND is conducting a series of scenario-based games to better understand how governments and other institutions should prepare for and respond to potential artificial intelligence (AI) and artificial general intelligence (AGI) developments. These games are run through the Infinite Potential platform, and this report is part of a series of publications that present findings and insights derived from player feedback.

Each Infinite Potential game presents a plausible future scenario in which advances in AGI outpace governance, and players are asked to craft immediate and longer-term responses. The authors of this report synthesize observations from 26 games conducted between June 2025 and February 2026. Each game featured one of five scenarios: Business and Civil Society, Cyber Surprise, European Energy, Geopolitics of Energy on the Korean Peninsula, and Remote Control. They identify the key issues, desired capabilities and playbooks, and other recommendations that participants in these games believed would be necessary to navigate a period when social legitimacy, economic stability, and technical control might collapse. The findings aim to help policymakers, researchers, corporate leaders, civil society organizations, and the public understand the preparations needed before such an event, the decisions likely to matter most once such an event begins, and the playbooks required to navigate it successfully.

items.title: Assessing Chinese and U.S. Technology Diffusion Capacity
items.author: Conlan Ellis
items.summary: The U.S.-China tech rivalry hinges not only on innovation but also on achieving widespread technological diffusion in the economy. This report examines both countries’ capacity to convert technological progress into sustained productivity gains.
items.body:
Technological competition between the United States and China is a defining feature of contemporary strategic rivalry and will shape the future distribution of economic and geopolitical power. When considering this competition, the key question is not only, “Which country leads in technological innovation?” but also, “Which country is better able to diffuse technological advances across its economy and convert them into sustained productivity gains?” In this report, we examine the two countries’ potential technological diffusion capacity to understand the broader trajectory of U.S.-China competition.

To measure diffusion capacity, the authors develop an analytical framework comprising three components of national diffusion capacity: actors, linkages, and contextual factors. They then populate the framework using proxies that serve as metrics for each component. Finally, the authors conduct a country-level comparative assessment based on these metrics. They explore each metric through two dimensions of technology diffusion: production diffusion, which refers to the process through which a new technology spreads in the production and supply side of an economy, and adoption diffusion, which describes the spread of technology on the demand and use side of the economy.

This research was independently initiated and conducted within the China Research Center within the RAND Global and Emerging Risks division using a gift from philanthropist Michael Tang, as well as gifts from other RAND supporters and income from operations.

items.title: Infinite Potential—Insights from the European Games
items.author: Anton Shenk
items.summary: The authors synthesize observations from tabletop games on artificial intelligence conducted in Europe or with European scenarios and identify the key issues and capabilities that players deemed necessary to navigate AI’s potential adverse effects.
items.body:
The RAND Center for the Geopolitics of AGI has conducted a series of scenario-based games to better understand how governments and other institutions should prepare for and respond to potential artificial intelligence (AI) and artificial general intelligence (AGI) developments. These games are run on the Infinite Potential platform, and this report is part of a series of publications that present findings and insights derived from player feedback.

Each Infinite Potential game presents a plausible future scenario in which advances in AGI outpace governance and asks players to craft immediate and longer-term responses. The authors of this report synthesize observations from 17 games conducted in Europe, or with European scenarios, between October 2025 and February 2026. They identify the key issues, capabilities, and playbooks that players deemed necessary for Europe to navigate the potential implications of adverse AI effects. The findings are aimed at helping policymakers, researchers, corporate leaders, civil organizations, and the public understand the preparations needed before such scenarios occur, the decisions likely to matter most once any of them begin, and the required playbooks to navigate successfully through each scenario.

items.title: Mapping Complex Legislation
items.author: Kara Jia
items.summary: The authors applied RAND’s U.S. Code Analysis Tool (CAT) to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as a proof of concept to show how CAT can support rapid statutory triage by identifying which statutory changes warrant closer review.
items.body:
Federal legislation is difficult to evaluate quickly because the U.S. Code is highly interconnected. A change to one provision can affect definitions, eligibility rules, cross-references, and implementation requirements elsewhere in federal law. In this short report, the authors applied RAND’s U.S. Code Analysis Tool (CAT) to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025 (OBBBA), which made 634 edits across 20 titles of the U.S. Code. CAT mapped these edits onto a graph of statutory provisions and cross-references to identify provisions that are highly connected, newly created, deleted, heavily edited, or substantially changed in their relationship to other parts of the code.

This report uses OBBBA as a proof of concept to show how CAT can support rapid statutory triage. CAT adds a different perspective from Congressional Budget Office scoring, policy-area summaries, or edit counts. It shows where edits sit within the broader structure of the code and whether those edits affect provisions that are central to statutory interpretation, program administration, or downstream implementation. For this retrospective analysis, the authors linked CAT-flagged provisions to Congressional Budget Office estimates (where available) for fiscal context. The analysis shows that CAT identified both headline OBBBA provisions (such as the Child Tax Credit and the new deduction for qualified tips) and less visible changes with potential implementation significance (including changes to Medicaid state-plan requirements, assisted housing restrictions, and agricultural program rules).

items.title: US removes B-1 bombers from UK base amid security concerns
items.author: Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Reuters
items.summary: The United States removed its B-1 bombers from a U.K. air base one week after several men were arrested there on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The United States removed its B-1 bombers from a U.K. air base one week after several men were arrested there on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a Pentagon official said on Sunday.

A dozen B-1 bombers were stationed at RAF Fairford air base, located northwest of London. The planes had been used for U.S. strikes on Iran.

“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesman wrote in an email.

Britain has “strong indications” that Iran was involved in a suspected plot targeting the base, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday. Iran said accusations linking Tehran to the alleged plan were baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran over the issue.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that the aircraft were removed from the base amid security concerns over suspected terror plots against the facility.

The British government had allowed the U.S. to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

U.S. President Donald Trump said those involved in the plot had planned “big damage” while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also pointed to the “hands of a foreign actor.”

items.title: Cocaine trafficking through seaports
items.author: Stijn Hoorens
items.summary: This report compares cocaine trafficking through Rotterdam and Le Havre, showing how organised crime exploits port logistics, corruption and digital systems, and why European ports need coordinated security, intelligence sharing and resilience.
items.body:
Europe's largest seaports are built to move goods quickly, efficiently and at immense scale. Yet these same strengths can be exploited by criminal networks, which use port facilities and logistics systems to support increasingly adaptive, transnational and technologically sophisticated cocaine trafficking operations.

This report examines how cocaine trafficking operates through the Port of Rotterdam and compares Rotterdam's vulnerabilities and responses with those identified in a parallel case study of the Port of Le Havre. Drawing on a targeted literature review and interviews with stakeholders involved in port security, logistics and enforcement, the study analyses the modus operandi, criminal actors and governance challenges that shape cocaine trafficking through one of Europe's largest maritime gateways.

Trafficking through Rotterdam has evolved in response to tighter physical security and digital container-release reforms. As traditional rip-on/rip-off methods have declined, criminal networks have shifted towards smaller shipments, cover cargo and reefer containers, peripheral logistics nodes, and manipulation of digital systems. Corruption remains a structural enabler, but its form differs between Rotterdam and Le Havre: Rotterdam faces distributed vulnerabilities across technical, logistical and IT roles, while Le Havre's labour-controlled structure creates concentrated risks around docker access and coercion.

The comparison shows that enforcement alone is insufficient to disrupt trafficking networks that operate across the Northern Range as an integrated corridor. Effective responses require coordinated European action, harmonised digital security standards, cross-border intelligence sharing, stronger oversight of high-risk roles and logistics nodes, and prevention efforts that build resilience among port workers and communities vulnerable to criminal recruitment.

Trafficking methods are becoming more adaptive

In Rotterdam, traditional rip-on/rip-off extraction has become less common as physical security and digital release systems have improved. Criminal networks increasingly use cover cargo, reefer containers, empty depots, smaller fragmented shipments and inland logistics hubs to facilitate their operations.

Corruption is central to how trafficking networks operate

Both Rotterdam and Le Havre show that insider assistance is fundamental to cocaine trafficking, but also that corruption takes different forms depending on a port's structure, labour arrangements and local culture. In Rotterdam, corruption risks are distributed across terminal, logistics, maintenance and IT roles. In Le Havre, the docker workforce's control over container movement creates a more concentrated point of leverage.

Port-level responses need to be integrated and transnational

Rotterdam's experiences with multi-agency cooperation, public-private information sharing, physical security reforms and resilience programmes show how layered governance can reduce specific vulnerabilities. However, traffickers adapt quickly and shift between ports, hinterland routes and secondary logistics nodes. European ports therefore need to work towards harmonised digital security, intelligence sharing and coordinated action against networks rather than isolated enforcement.

This research was funded by the Interministerial Program of Research Applied to the Fight for Combatting Drugs (PIRALAD) and conducted within RAND Europe.

items.title: All B-1 Bombers Leave RAF Fairford in Hasty Departure from UK Base
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: All 12 American bombers deployed in Britain rapidly returned to the U.S. on Oct. 4 following security concerns about a potential Iranian threat to their base in the U.K. The post All B-1 Bombers Leave RAF Fairford in Hasty Departure from UK Base appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
All 12 American bombers deployed in Britain rapidly returned to the U.S. on Oct. 4 following security concerns about a potential Iranian threat to their base in the U.K.

The dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which were stationed at RAF Fairford amid ongoing hostilities with Iran, departed over the course of a day, local aircraft spotters said. The U.S. military later confirmed the unexpected departure of the aircraft.

“All U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States,” the Pentagon and U.S. European Command said in statements to Air & Space Forces Magazine.

The U.S. military emphasized that bombers could still strike targets across the globe from the continental United States—something B-1B, B-2 Spirit, and B-52 Stratofortress bombers all did during the height of operations against Iran this spring.

“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities—including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States—anywhere, anytime,” the statement read.

Still, stationing bombers at RAF Fairford sharply reduced the flight time U.S. bombers needed to strike targets in Iran. The open-source group Military Air Tracking Alliance recorded 29 separate bombers that deployed to RAF Fairford, located in southwest England, at different points during the conflict.

The departure of the last 12 bombers comes a week after arrests were made following a suspected plot against the base. Six people have been arrested in connection with the episode. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “strong indications” that Iran was behind the threat.

Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer allowed the U.S. to use the base to attack Iran for what the U.K. government called defensive strikes. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July it considered RAF Fairford a legitimate target because of the U.S. bombers deployed there.

At the height of the deployment, which began in early March during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. had around two dozen bombers deployed to RAF Fairford at a single time—some 18 B-1B and half a dozen B-52H bombers. Since the U.S. reached a shaky ceasefire with Iran in April, the bombers have mostly conducted training missions, and the B-52s left months ago. One B-1B that arrived just last week to replace another bomber was part of the exodus on Oct. 4.

RAF Fairford does not have permanent assigned U.S. Air Force aircraft, but the base has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.

The Air Force permanently stations aircraft in the U.K. at RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath also serves as a stopover for fighters heading to and from the Middle East from the U.S. Nearby, RAF Mildenhall hosts KC-135 tankers that belong to the 100th Air Refueling Wing stationed at the base.

The U.S. has also been rotating its fighters based in the Middle East, sending fresh F-16 Fighting Falcon and F-35 units to the region, primarily from the Air National Guard.

items.title: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
items.author: Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari and Eman Abouhassira, Reuters
items.summary: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.
items.body:
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The government’s armed forces would press the offensive “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. A military spokesman later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons.

The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen’s capital Sanaa and vast parts of the northwest, where most of the population live, since 2014. They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies, and have updated their weaponry with the help of Iran.

The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and some 90 miles of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route.

That advance also opened a new front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran’s responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

HOUTHIS SAY THEY STRUCK SAUDI ARABIA

As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council, made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia.

They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.

Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted.

He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen’s regional allies and international partners to support PLC forces and institutions.

Regional and Western officials told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.

NEW FRONT IN MIDEAST WAR

The U.S. is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.

The United States’ war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East and depleted crucial military hardware.

Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups and factions backed by competing regional and international actors.

After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi’ite Muslims, captured Sanaa.

The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also recognized by the United Nations, has, since the Houthi takeover, controlled the south and east of the country, based in the former South Yemen capital of Aden.

Saudi Arabia entered Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis.

A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen’s Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast.

Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen’s third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.

The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.

Three in four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.
